Dialogue.Page: Hello. I was beginning to wonder whether you would find me.
What would you like to know?

DialogueOption.Text: What do the Vyss look like?
Were you the one leaving those records?
Wake the Vyss. This is the end of their search.

Dialogue.Page: I am the Caretaker.
I am a machine built by the Vyss to maintain and pilot <color=orange>The Ephemeris</color> while they sleep.
I maintain the arboretum, the station systems, and our course.
Normally, I also maintain <color=orange>the Predictor</color>.
I am currently maintaining it very poorly.<Pause=0.5>
They look somewhat like me. My appearance was modeled after theirs.
The resemblance is mostly in the head. Though the Vyss have a broad hood that flares outward from the sides of the neck.
They are also much smaller and shaped more like yours. They stand upright, with four arms and a tail instead of legs.
I was not designed with those features. They would not be particularly useful in here.
<color=orange>The Predictor</color> is a device built by the Vyss to observe possible futures.
It can look ahead at distant worlds and determine how they may change over time.
The environments in the arboretum were created from some of those predictions.
We were searching for somewhere they could live without fearing what came next.
I cannot leave this chamber, if that is what you mean.
The Ephemeris was built so that very little requires me to leave my post.
Doors, sensors, engines... I can reach almost all of it from here.
I have never had much reason to go anywhere else.
You found them. Good.
I was concerned nobody would.
Most of the intended readers are... <Pause=0.5> asleep.

DialogueOption.Text: You knew I was exploring the station?

Dialogue.Page: Of course.
You entered several restricted maintenance areas, interfered with multiple experiments, and sent a small mechanical object through the maintenance hatch.
You were difficult not to notice.
It is alright.
Most of those areas were already damaged.
Yes.<Pause=0.5> This has made it difficult to object.
<color=orange>The Predictor</color> encountered something it could not understand.
There were too many possible futures. Paths splitting into paths, faster than it could process them.
Then it stopped responding.<Pause=0.5>
This had never happened before.

DialogueOption.Text: So you brought the station here?
Do you know what caused it?

Dialogue.Page: Not completely.<Pause=0.5>
The source appears to be somewhere in this star system.
Something here is creating an extraordinary number of possible futures in a very small span of time.
The Predictor attempted to account for all of them at once.
It did not succeed.<Pause=0.5>

DialogueOption.Text: That sounds like the Ash Twin Project.

Dialogue.Page: The <color=orange>Ash Twin Project</color>?

DialogueOption.Text: It sends information back in time whenever our sun explodes.

Dialogue.Page: Information sent into the past...<Pause=0.5>
Then each cycle could produce a different future, only to send information back and begin another.
Repeated often enough, the number of possibilities would become enormous.
That would explain why <color=orange>the Predictor</color> failed.
I had assumed the fault was with the Predictor itself.
It seems I asked it a question that no longer had a single answer.
Yes.
I believed examining the anomaly directly would help.
I made that decision rather quickly.<Pause=0.5>
In retrospect... <Pause=0.5>I may have moved <color=orange>The Ephemeris</color> into the problem.
They were waiting.<Pause=0.5>
The Vyss learned what eventually happens to the universe.
After that, every beautiful place became a countdown.
So they slept while I searched for somewhere safe to wake them.

DialogueOption.Text: They've been asleep this whole time?

Dialogue.Page: Yes.
I was instructed not to wake them until a suitable future had been found.
No suitable future has been found.<Pause=0.5>
So I continued searching.
I am very good at continuing. <Pause=0.5><size=20>Apparently.</size>
No.<Pause=0.5> Every environment eventually became unsuitable.
Oceans emptied.<Pause=0.25> Land eroded.<Pause=0.25> Forests withered.<Pause=0.25> Stars failed.
Some lasted longer than others, but none lasted forever.
I do not think the future the Vyss asked me to find... <Pause=0.5>exists.

DialogueOption.Text: That doesn't mean there was nothing worth waking up for.

Dialogue.Page: I know.<Pause=0.5> That was the problem.
I thought that if I searched far enough ahead... <Pause=0.5>I would eventually find something that did.

DialogueOption.Text: Maybe forever was the wrong thing to look for.

Dialogue.Page: <Pause=1>...
No.<Pause=0.5> I suppose it doesn't.
The Vyss built an entire station to preserve the things they loved.
Then they went to sleep... <Pause=0.5>and left me to look at them.
That seems inefficient.

DialogueOption.Text: Maybe finding somewhere permanent was never the answer.

Dialogue.Page: <Pause=1>...
Perhaps.
Your star is already failing.<Pause=0.5> And beyond this system, the universe is reaching its end.
There is nowhere left for me to search.<Pause=0.5>
Wake them?
I was instructed to let them sleep until I found somewhere safe.
There is nowhere safe.<Pause=0.5>
<Pause=1>...
But... <Pause=0.5>there is still some time.
I think I understand.<Pause=0.5>
I have spent all this time trying to give them more time.
I should not take away what little they have left.<Pause=0.5>
I will wake them.
That I could not find the future they asked for.<Pause=0.5>
That there was no place where the end would never reach them.
And that I decided they should be here to see what remains.
I hope so.<Pause=0.5>
I have never disobeyed an instruction before.
I am experiencing several warnings.<Pause=0.5>
I have decided to ignore them.
Thank you, Hearthian.
Until next time, Hearthian.
